title: Single Number
problem: Every element in a non-empty integer array appears exactly twice except for one element, which appears once. Find that single element using linear time and constant extra space.
example: Explanation: 1 and 2 appear twice; 4 appears once.
intuition: XOR has three properties that make this trivial: a ^ a = 0, a ^ 0 = a, and XOR is commutative and associative. So if you XOR every number together, each pair cancels to 0 no matter where the two copies sit, and only the lonely number survives.
notes: Say it like this: "A hash map of counts works in O(n) time and O(n) space. Since x XOR x is 0 and XOR is order- independent, XORing everything leaves only the single number: O(n) time, O(1) space."
Edge cases: single-element array; negative numbers (XOR works on the two's complement bits, so fine).
Common mistakes: starting res at something other than 0; trying sort-based solutions when O(1) space and O(n) time are both required.
Follow-ups: "What if every other number appears three times?" Count bits mod 3 (Single Number II, 15.8). "Two single numbers?" Split by a differing bit (Single Number III, 15.9). 15.2
simple: Every number appears twice except one. Find it.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Count each value using a hash map.
Return the value whose count is 1.
approaches.why: One pass to count and one pass over the map; the map holds up to n/2 + 1 keys.
approaches.simple: Count with a map.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Start with res = 0.
XOR every number into res. Pairs cancel.
Return res.
approaches.why: One pass, one integer of state.
approaches.simple: XOR everything together; pairs cancel out to 0, leaving the single number.

title: Number of 1 Bits
problem: Given a positive integer n, return the number of set bits (1s) in its binary representation. This is also called the Hamming weight.
example: Explanation: 11 in binary is 1011, which has three 1 bits.
intuition: The simple way is to look at every bit: check the last bit with n & 1, then shift right. That always costs 32 steps.

The better trick: n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit. Subtracting 1 flips the lowest 1 to 0 and turns every 0 below it into 1, so the AND wipes out exactly that one bit. Repeat until n is 0 and count the steps; the loop runs once per set bit. Example: 1011 → 1010 → 1000 → 0000, three steps.
notes: Say it like this: "I can check all 32 bits with shifts, which is constant but always 32 steps. Using n & (n-1), which removes the lowest set bit, the loop runs only as many times as there are 1 bits."
Edge cases: n = 0 gives 0; in Java an "unsigned" input like 11111111111111111111111111111101 arrives as a negative int, so loop on n!= 0, not n > 0.
Common mistakes: using >> instead of >>> in Java with a while (n!= 0) shift loop; arithmetic shift keeps copying the sign bit and the loop never ends for negative input.
Follow-ups: "Built-in?" Integer.bitCount(n) in Java. "Many queries?" Precompute counts for all 8-bit or 16- bit values and add up table lookups. 15.3
simple: Count the 1 bits in a number.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each of the 32 bit positions, check (n >> i) & 1.
Add it to the count.
approaches.why: Always exactly 32 iterations regardless of input.
approaches.simple: Check all 32 bit positions.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: While n!= 0: do n &= n - 1 and increment the count.
Return the count.
approaches.time: O(k) where k = number of set bits (at most 32)
approaches.why: Each iteration removes exactly one set bit.
approaches.simple: n & (n − 1) removes the lowest 1 bit; count how many times you can do that.

title: Counting Bits
problem: Given an integer n, return an array ans of length n + 1 where ans[i] is the number of 1 bits in the binary form of i, for every i from 0 to n.
intuition: Calling a popcount on every number costs O(log i) each. But the bit count of i is closely related to a smaller number we have already computed. i >> 1 is i without its last bit, so ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1). Since i >> 1 < i, the answer is already in the table. This is a tiny DP over numbers.
(Equivalent alternative: ans[i] = ans[i & (i - 1)] + 1, using "drop the lowest set bit".)
notes: Say it like this: "Counting bits per number is O(n log n). Because i >> 1 is i without its last bit, ans[i] = ans[i>>1] + (i&1) gives each value in O(1), so O(n) overall."
Edge cases: n = 0 returns [0].
Common mistakes: array of size n instead of n + 1; operator precedence in Java/JS (ans[i >> 1] + i & 1 parses as (ans[i>>1] + i) & 1); always bracket (i & 1).
Follow-ups: "Another recurrence?" ans[i] = ans[i & (i-1)] + 1, or using the most recent power of two: ans[i] = 1 + ans[i - highestPowerOf2]. 15.4
simple: For every number from 0 to n, count its 1 bits.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each i from 0 to n, count its bits with the n & (n - 1) loop.
approaches.why: Each number has at most log2(n) + 1 bits to clear.
approaches.simple: Count bits for each number separately.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: For i from 1 to n: ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1).
approaches.why: Each entry is computed in O(1) from a smaller, already-filled entry.
approaches.simple: Bits of i = bits of i / 2 plus the last bit of i.

title: Reverse Bits
problem: Reverse the bits of a 32-bit unsigned integer: bit 0 becomes bit 31, bit 1 becomes bit 30, and so on. Return the resulting number.
example: Explanation: The 32-bit string is read backwards.
intuition: Think of it like reversing a number digit by digit, but in base 2. Take the last bit of n, push it into the result from the right (shift result left, OR the bit in), then drop that bit from n. After exactly 32 rounds, the first bit you read (bit 0) has been shifted all the way to bit 31.
The key detail is that you must do 32 iterations, not "until n is zero", or leading zeros of the result are lost.
notes: Say it like this: "The string approach pads to 32 bits, reverses and parses. The bitwise way pulls the last bit off n and pushes it onto res 32 times. Both are O(1) because the width is fixed, but the bitwise one avoids allocation."
Edge cases: n = 0; inputs with the top bit set (negative in Java); results above 2^31 − 1 must be unsigned in JS (>>> 0).
Common mistakes: looping while (n!= 0) (loses trailing positions); using >> in Java so the sign bit smears in.

Follow-ups: "Called many times?" Cache reversed bytes in a 256-entry table and combine four lookups, or use the divide-and-conquer swap (swap 16-bit halves, then 8-bit, 4, 2, 1 with masks). Java has Integer.reverse(n). 15.5
simple: Reverse the 32 bits of a number.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Convert n to a 32-character binary string padded with zeros.
Reverse the string and parse it back as an unsigned integer.
approaches.why: A fixed-length string of 32 characters.
approaches.simple: Write it as a 32-character binary string, reverse it, and read it back.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: res = 0.
Repeat 32 times: res = (res << 1) | (n & 1); then n >>>= 1.
Return res (in JS, res >>> 0 to view it as unsigned).
approaches.why: Fixed 32 iterations with two integers of state.
approaches.simple: 32 times: shift the answer left and drop in the lowest bit of n, then shift n right.

title: Missing Number
problem: An array contains n distinct numbers from the range [0, n]. Exactly one number in the range is missing. Return it.
example: Explanation: n = 3, range is 0..3, and 2 is absent.
intuition: If nothing were missing, the array would hold every value 0..n. So pair each expected value with what is present. XOR all indices 0..n together with all array values: every present number appears twice (once as an index or n, once as a value) and cancels, leaving the missing one.
The sum trick works the same way: n(n+1)/2 − sum(nums). XOR is preferred because it can never overflow; with sums, use long if n can be large.
notes: Say it like this: "Sorting and scanning is O(n log n); a hash set is O(n) time and space. XORing every index 0..n with every value cancels all present numbers, giving O(n) time and O(1) space without overflow risk."
Edge cases: missing 0 ([1] → 0); missing n ([0,1] → 2); single element.
Common mistakes: forgetting to include n itself (start res at n); sum formula overflow in int for large n.
Follow-ups: "Array is sorted?" Binary search for the first index where nums[i]!= i, O(log n). "One missing and one repeated?" See 15.10. 15.6
simple: Numbers 0..n with one missing. Find it.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Sort the array.
The first index i where nums[i]!= i is the answer; if none, the answer is n.
approaches.why: Sorting dominates; the scan is linear.
approaches.simple: Sort and find the first position that doesn't hold its own index.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Put every number in a hash set.
Check 0..n and return the first value not in the set.
approaches.why: Linear inserts and lookups, but the set stores n values.
approaches.simple: Put numbers in a set and check 0..n.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Start with res = n.
For each index i: res ^= i ^ nums[i].
Return res.
approaches.why: Single pass; all present values cancel against their matching index.
approaches.simple: XOR all indices and all values; everything cancels except the missing number.

title: Sum of Two Integers
problem: Return the sum of two integers a and b without using the + or - operators. Inputs are in the range [-1000, 1000].
intuition: This is how a hardware adder works. When you add two bits: - The sum bit (ignoring carry) is a ^ b (1 when exactly one is 1). - The carry is a & b, and it goes into the next position, so it is (a & b) << 1.

So a + b = (a ^ b) + ((a & b) << 1). That still has a +, but we can apply the same rule again to the new pair, repeating until the carry becomes 0. Each round pushes the carry at least one position left, so in 32-bit arithmetic it finishes in at most 32 rounds. Negative numbers work for free because two's complement addition is the same bit operation.
notes: Say it like this: "XOR gives the sum without carries and AND shifted left gives the carries. I repeat a = a^b, b = (a&b)<<1 until there is no carry, at most 32 rounds, so O(1)."
Edge cases: negative numbers (-1 + 1), zero operands.

Common mistakes: computing a ^ b into a before computing the carry from the old a; in Python this loops forever on negatives because ints are unbounded (Java/JS are fine because they are fixed 32-bit for bitwise ops).
Follow-ups: "Subtraction?" a - b = a + (~b + 1), using the same adder for the + 1. 15.7
simple: Add two integers without using + or −.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Without + or -, the honest "brute force" is to simulate addition bit by bit like grade-school addition with an explicit carry.
steps: For each bit position 0..31, read bit x of a and y of b.
Sum bit = x ^ y ^ carry; new carry = majority of (x, y, carry).
Set the sum bit into the result.
approaches.why: Always 32 positions.
approaches.simple: Add bit by bit like a hardware adder, tracking the carry.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: While b!= 0: - carry = (a & b) << 1 - a = a ^ b - b = carry
Return a.
approaches.why: The carry shifts left every round, so at most 32 rounds.
approaches.simple: XOR gives the sum without carries; AND shifted left gives the carries. Repeat until no carry is left.

title: Reverse Integer
problem: Given a signed 32-bit integer x, return x with its digits reversed. If the reversed value is outside the signed 32-bit range [−2^31, 2^31 − 1], return 0. Assume you cannot store 64-bit integers.
example: Explanation: Digits reversed, sign kept. 1534236469 would return 0 (overflow).
intuition: Pop the last digit with x % 10, push it onto the result with res * 10 + digit, then x /= 10. In Java and JS (with Math.trunc), % keeps the sign of x, so negative numbers work with the same loop.

The real question is overflow. Before doing res * 10 + digit, check whether it would cross the limits: if res > MAX / 10, or res == MAX / 10 and digit > 7, it overflows (MAX = 2147483647 ends in 7). The negative side is symmetric with MIN / 10 and digit < -8.
notes: Say it like this: "The string approach reverses and parses into a long, but that uses 64-bit storage. Instead I pop and push digits arithmetically and check for overflow before each push by comparing to INT_MAX/10 and INT_MIN/10. That is O(number of digits) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: x = 0; trailing zeros (120 → 21); Integer.MIN_VALUE (Math.abs overflows in int, so the brute force casts to long first); results just past the limit like 1534236469.
Common mistakes: checking overflow after the multiplication (by then the int has already wrapped); in JS using Math.floor for negatives (rounds the wrong way).
Follow-ups: "Palindrome number?" Reverse half the digits and compare, which also avoids overflow. 15.8
simple: Reverse the digits of an integer; return 0 if it overflows 32 bits.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Convert |x| to a string, reverse it.
Parse it as a 64-bit long, reapply the sign, and return 0 if it is outside int range. (This violates the "no 64-bit" constraint, which is exactly why the interviewer asks for the next approach.)
approaches.time: O(d) where d = number of digits (≤ 10)
approaches.why: String of at most 10 characters.
approaches.simple: Reverse it as a string and check the range.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: res = 0.
While x!= 0: digit = x % 10; x /= 10 (truncating).
Before pushing, check overflow against MAX/10 and MIN/10; return 0 if it would overflow.
res = res * 10 + digit.
approaches.why: One iteration per digit, at most 10.
approaches.simple: Pop digits from the end and push them onto the answer, checking for overflow before each push.

title: Single Number - II
problem: Every element in an integer array appears exactly three times except one, which appears exactly once. Find the single element in linear time and constant extra space.
example: Explanation: 0 and 1 appear three times each; 99 appears once.
intuition: XOR no longer helps because three copies of x XOR to x, not 0. Go one level lower and look at each bit position separately. For a given bit, every tripled number contributes its bit 0 or 3 times, so the total count of 1s at that position is 3k plus the single number's bit. Therefore count % 3 is exactly the single number's bit there. Doing this for 32 positions rebuilds the answer.

The optimal version does the same "count mod 3" for all 32 bits in parallel with two masks, ones and twos. A bit is in ones if it has been seen 1 time (mod 3), in twos if seen 2 times. When a number arrives: - ones = (ones ^ x) & ~twos — add x's bits to ones, unless they are already in twos. - twos = (twos ^ x) & ~ones — move bits into twos, unless they just landed in ones. On the third occurrence a bit leaves both masks, which is the "reset to 0" of mod 3. At the end, ones holds the single number.
notes: Say it like this: "A hash map is O(n) space. Counting each bit position mod 3 gives the single number's bits in O(32n) time and O(1) space. The ones/twos masks run that mod-3 counter for all bits at once in a single pass."
Edge cases: negative single number (bit 31 must be handled, which the bit loop does); array of length 1.
Common mistakes: updating twos using the old ones (the order of the two lines matters); using >>> vs >> doesn't matter here since we mask with & 1, but forgetting bit 31 does.
Follow-ups: "Every number appears k times except one?" Count bits mod k (Approach 2 generalises directly). Sorting and checking triples is another O(n log n), O(1) option. 15.9
simple: Every number appears three times except one. Find it.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Count frequencies in a hash map.
Return the key with count 1.
approaches.why: One counting pass; the map holds about n/3 keys.
approaches.simple: Count with a map.

approaches.label: Better
steps: For each bit position b in 0..31, count how many numbers have that bit set.
If count % 3 == 1, set bit b in the answer.
approaches.why: 32 passes over the array, constant state. Already meets the constraints; Approach 3 just removes the 32x factor.
approaches.simple: For each bit, count how many numbers have it set; if the count isn't a multiple of 3, the single number has that bit.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: ones = 0, twos = 0.
For each x: ones = (ones ^ x) & ~twos; twos = (twos ^ x) & ~ones.
Return ones.
approaches.why: One pass, two masks; each bit runs a tiny mod-3 counter in parallel.
approaches.simple: Two masks (ones, twos) track bits seen once and twice; a bit seen three times is cleared.

title: Single Number - III
problem: In an integer array, exactly two elements appear once and every other element appears exactly twice. Return the two single elements in any order, using linear time and constant extra space.
example: Explanation: 1 and 2 appear twice; 3 and 5 appear once.
intuition: XOR everything and you get xor = a ^ b, the XOR of the two singles. Since a!= b, xor has at least one set bit, and at that bit a and b differ. Pick any such bit (the lowest is easy: xor & -xor).

Now split the whole array into two groups: numbers with that bit set and numbers without. a and b land in different groups, and every duplicate pair lands together in the same group. XOR each group separately and each collapses to one single number.
Trace: XOR of [1,2,1,3,2,5] = 3 ^ 5 = 110. Lowest set bit = 010. Group with bit: 2,3,2 → 3. Group without: 1,1,5 → 5.
notes: Say it like this: "A hash map is O(n) space. XOR of everything is a^b; any set bit in it separates a from b, so I partition the array by that bit and XOR each half, which isolates each single in O(n) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: one of the singles is 0; negative numbers; xor = Integer.MIN_VALUE (in Java -xor overflows back to MIN_VALUE, and MIN & MIN is still the correct bit, so it's safe).
Common mistakes: testing (x & diff) == 1 instead of!= 0 (diff is usually not bit 0); in languages with big ints (Python), -xor behaves differently but still works.
Follow-ups: "Why any set bit, not just the lowest?" Any bit where a and b differ works; the lowest is just cheapest to extract. 15.10
simple: Two numbers appear once, all others twice. Find both.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Count frequencies with a hash map.
Collect the two keys with count 1.
approaches.why: Map holds up to n/2 + 1 keys.
approaches.simple: Count with a map.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: xor = XOR of all numbers (= a ^ b).
diff = xor & -xor (lowest bit where a and b differ).
XOR numbers with (x & diff)!= 0 into a, the rest into b.
Return [a, b].
approaches.why: Two passes, a few integers.
approaches.simple: XOR everything to get a ^ b, take one bit where they differ, and split the numbers by that bit into two groups that each XOR to one answer.

title: Find the repeating and missing number
problem: You are given an array of size n containing numbers from 1 to n. One number A appears twice and one number B is missing; everything else appears exactly once. Return [A, B] (repeating first, then missing).
example: Explanation: 3 appears twice and 4 is missing from 1..5.
intuition: Compare the array to the ideal array 1..n. Let x = A (repeating) and y = B (missing). - Sum difference: S − Sn = x − y, where S is the actual sum and Sn = n(n+1)/2. - Square-sum difference: S2 − S2n = x² − y² = (x − y)(x + y).

Two equations, two unknowns: divide the second by the first to get x + y, then x = ((x−y) + (x+y)) / 2 and y = x − (x − y). Use long because the sum of squares for n = 10^5 is about 3·10^14, way past int.

The XOR alternative (same idea as Single Number III): XOR all values and 1..n gives x ^ y; split by a differing bit; then do one more scan to see which of the two candidates actually appears in the array. It avoids overflow entirely.
notes: Say it like this: "Counting each value by scanning is O(n²); a frequency array makes it O(n) time and O(n) space. Using the differences of sum and sum of squares against 1..n gives x−y and x²−y², which solve for both numbers in O(n) time and O(1) space; I use long for the squares."
Edge cases: n = 2 ([1,1] → [1,2], [2,2] → [2,1]); missing number is n or 1.
Common mistakes: int overflow on v * v and on n(n+1)(2n+1) (cast to long first); returning [missing, repeating] in the wrong order.

Follow-ups: "Avoid overflow entirely?" Use the XOR method: XOR all values with 1..n to get x^y, split both the array and 1..n by its lowest set bit into two XOR buckets, then scan once to see which candidate occurs in the array (that one is repeating). "Can you modify the array?" Mark visited indices by negating nums[|v| − 1]; seeing an already negative slot reveals the repeat. LeetCode 2965 (Find Missing and Repeated Values) is the same problem on an n×n grid with values 1..n². 15.11
simple: Numbers 1..n with one repeated and one missing. Find both.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For each value v in 1..n, count how many times it appears by scanning the array.
Count 2 → repeating; count 0 → missing.
approaches.why: n values, each counted with a full scan.
approaches.simple: Count each value by scanning.

approaches.label: Better
steps: Make a frequency array freq of size n + 1.
Count every value.
Scan 1..n: freq == 2 → repeating, freq == 0 → missing.
approaches.why: Two linear passes; the frequency array has n + 1 slots.
approaches.simple: Use a frequency array.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Compute Sn = n(n+1)/2 and S2n = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 as long.
Compute actual S and S2 (as long).
d1 = S − Sn (= x − y), d2 = S2 − S2n (= x² − y²), so sum = d2 / d1 (= x + y).
x = (d1 + sum) / 2, y = x − d1.
approaches.why: One pass for the two sums, then constant math.
approaches.simple: Compare the real sum and sum of squares with the expected ones; the two differences give two equations.

title: Rabin Karp Algorithm
problem: Given a text text and a pattern pattern, return every starting index (0-based) at which pattern occurs in text, using the Rabin-Karp rolling-hash idea. (GFG's version of this problem prints 1-based indices; just add 1.)
intuition: The naive method compares the pattern against every window of length m character by character, which is O(n·m). Rabin-Karp instead turns each window into a number (a hash) and compares numbers in O(1). Only when the hashes match do we compare characters, to rule out a collision.

The trick that makes it fast is the rolling hash. Treat a window as a number in base B: hash("abc") = a·B² + b·B + c (mod a prime M). To slide right by one character, remove the leftmost character's contribution text[i]·B^(m−1), multiply by B to shift everything one place, and add the new character. That is O(1) per slide, so all n − m + 1 windows are hashed in O(n).
With a large prime modulus collisions are rare, so expected time is O(n + m). Worst case (adversarial collisions) degrades to O(n·m) because of the verification step.
notes: Say it like this: "Naive matching compares every window, O(n·m). Rabin-Karp hashes each window with a polynomial rolling hash that updates in O(1) per slide, and only compares characters on a hash match, giving O(n + m) expected time; the worst case is still O(n·m) if many collisions occur."
Edge cases: pattern longer than text; empty pattern; pattern equal to text; overlapping matches ("aaa" in "aaaaa").

Common mistakes: negative values after subtraction (add M before taking mod); int overflow in Java (use long); skipping the verification step and reporting false matches; precision loss in JS if M·B exceeds 2^53.

Follow-ups: "Reduce collisions?" Use double hashing (two different moduli) and treat a match as both agreeing. "Where is it better than KMP?" Searching many patterns of the same length at once (put pattern hashes in a set), plagiarism detection, and substring problems like Longest Duplicate Substring with binary search. 15.12
simple: Find every place a pattern occurs in a text, using hashing.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For every start i from 0 to n − m, compare text[i..i+m−1] with the pattern character by character.
Record i on a full match.
approaches.why: Each of the n − m + 1 windows can take up to m comparisons.
approaches.simple: Compare the pattern at every start position.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Choose base B = 256 and prime M = 1_000_000_007. Precompute h = B^(m−1) mod M.
Compute the hash of the pattern and of the first window.
For each window start i: if the hashes match, verify character by character and record i.
Roll: win = ((win − text[i]·h) · B + text[i+m]) mod M, keeping it non-negative.
approaches.time: O(n + m) expected, O(n·m) worst case
approaches.why: Each slide is O(1); character checks happen only on hash matches (real matches plus rare collisions).
approaches.simple: Rabin-Karp: give each window a number (rolling hash) and update it in O(1) as the window slides; compare text only when the numbers match.

title: Z function
problem: For a string s, the Z-array is defined as Z[i] = length of the longest substring starting at i that is also a prefix of s (with Z[0] usually set to 0). Compute it in linear time, and use it to find every starting index (0-based) of pattern in text.
example: Explanation: combined = "abc$xabcabzabc"; positions where Z = 3 map back to text indices 1 and 7.
intuition: To search, build combined = pattern + "$" + text, where $ is a character that appears in neither string. Any position in the text part whose Z-value equals m (pattern length) is a full match, because the substring starting there equals the first m characters, which is the pattern. The $ guarantees Z never exceeds m.

Computing Z naively costs O(n²): from each i, extend while characters match the prefix. The linear algorithm keeps a window [l, r]: the rightmost segment found so far that matches a prefix (s[l..r] == s[0..r−l]). For a new i inside the window, s[i..r] is a copy of s[i−l..r−l], so we already know Z[i] >= min(r − i + 1, Z[i − l]). Start from that value and only try to extend past r. Every successful extension moves r right, and r only moves right at most n times, so the whole thing is O(n).

Small trace on s = "aabxaab": Z = [0,1,0,0,3,1,0]. At i = 4 we extend to "aab" (length 3), window becomes [4,6]. At i = 5, inside the window, Z[5 − 4] = Z[1] = 1, r − i + 1 = 2, so start at 1; next char b vs a fails, Z[5] = 1 with no extra work.
notes: Say it like this: "Concatenate pattern, a separator, and text; any text position whose Z-value equals the pattern length is a match. Computing Z naively is quadratic, but keeping the rightmost matching window [l, r) lets me initialise each Z[i] from Z[i − l], and since r only moves right the whole thing is O(n + m)."

Edge cases: separator character appearing in the input (pick something impossible, or avoid concatenation by computing Z of the pattern and matching text separately); pattern longer than text; all-same-character strings (the worst case for the naive version).

Common mistakes: mixing inclusive and exclusive r (pick one convention and stick to it); forgetting the separator, which lets Z-values run past m; off-by-one when converting back to a text index (i − m − 1).

Follow-ups: "Z vs KMP?" Both are O(n + m); Z is often easier to derive, KMP streams the text without concatenation. Other uses: count distinct substrings, string compression period (smallest p with p + Z[p] == n and n % p == 0). 15.13
simple: Find pattern matches with the Z-function.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: Build combined.
For each i ≥ 1, count matching characters between combined[i..] and combined[0..] (naive Z).
Report i − m − 1 whenever Z[i] == m.
approaches.why: Each position may extend up to O(n + m) characters (e.g., all a s).
approaches.simple: For each position, count matching characters with the start of pattern$text directly.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Build s = pattern + "$" + text and an array z of length s.length.
Keep l = r = 0 (window [l, r) with r exclusive).
For each i ≥ 1: if i < r, set z[i] = min(r − i, z[i − l]). Then extend while s[z[i]] == s[i + z[i]].
If i + z[i] > r, update l = i, r = i + z[i].
Every i with z[i] == m gives a match at text index i − m − 1.
approaches.why: r only moves forward, so total extension work is linear; the Z-array stores one int per character.
approaches.simple: Z-function: reuse the rightmost match window [l, r] to skip comparisons; a Z value equal to the pattern length is a match.

title: KMP Algorithm or LPS array
problem: Given strings haystack and needle, return the index of the first occurrence of needle in haystack, or −1 if it does not occur (LeetCode 28). Solve it with the KMP algorithm, which is built on the LPS (longest proper prefix which is also suffix) array.
example: Explanation: "sad" occurs at 0 and 6; the first is 0. For needle = "aabaaab", LPS = [0,1,0,1,2,2,3].
intuition: When naive matching fails after matching j characters, it shifts the pattern by one and re-compares characters it has already seen. KMP asks: "of the j characters I just matched (which equal needle[0..j−1]), what is the longest proper prefix of the needle that is also a suffix of them?" That length is lps[j−1]. We can slide the needle so that prefix lines up with that suffix and continue comparing from there, without ever moving backward in the haystack.

lps[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of needle[0..i] that is also a suffix of it. For "aabaaab": at index 4 ("aabaa"), "aa" is both prefix and suffix, so lps = 2; at index 6 ("aabaaab"), "aab", so lps = 3.

Building LPS uses the same idea on the needle itself: keep len = current matched prefix length. If needle[i] == needle[len], extend (len++). On mismatch, fall back to len = lps[len − 1] and retry, without advancing i. Each fallback decreases len, and len grows at most once per i, so it's O(m) total. The search phase is the same loop with the haystack in place of the needle.
notes: Say it like this: "Naive matching is O(n·m) because it re-reads characters after a mismatch. KMP precomputes the LPS array of the needle so that on a mismatch it jumps the needle to the longest prefix that is also a suffix of what matched, never moving backward in the haystack. That's O(n + m) time and O(m) space."
Edge cases: empty needle (return 0 by convention); needle longer than haystack; repeated characters like "aaaa" (LPS = [0,1,2,3]).
Common mistakes: advancing i on a fallback in the LPS build (you must retry the same i); falling back to lps[len] instead of lps[len − 1]; using lps[i] = len before incrementing len.

Follow-ups: "All occurrences?" On a full match, record i − m and set j = lps[j − 1] to keep going (handles overlaps). Other LPS uses: Shortest Palindrome (15.14), Repeated Substring Pattern (n % (n − lps[n−1]) == 0), Longest Happy Prefix (lps[n−1]). 15.14
simple: Find the first place a needle occurs in a haystack.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For every start i in haystack, compare the needle character by character.
Return the first i with a full match, else −1.
approaches.why: Each start can compare up to m characters (e.g., haystack "aaaa…ab", needle "aaab").
approaches.simple: Try every start and compare.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: Build lps for the needle (as described above).
Scan the haystack with i (never moves back) and j (chars of needle matched).
If characters match, advance both; if j == m, return i − m.
On mismatch: if j > 0, set j = lps[j − 1] (keep i); else advance i.
approaches.why: LPS build is O(m), search is O(n) because i never moves backward and each fallback is paid for by an earlier advance; LPS array has m entries.
approaches.simple: KMP: precompute, for each prefix of the needle, the longest part that is both a prefix and a suffix. On a mismatch, jump using it instead of starting over.

title: Shortest Palindrome
problem: Given a string s, you may only add characters to its front. Return the shortest palindrome you can make this way.
example: Explanation: The longest palindromic prefix is "aacecaa"; prepend the reverse of the remaining "a".
intuition: Whatever we add goes in front, so some prefix of s must already be the "core" palindrome, and we prepend the reverse of the rest. To add as few characters as possible, we want the longest prefix of s that is a palindrome. Answer = reverse(s[k..]) + s, where k is that prefix's length.

How do we find the longest palindromic prefix fast? A prefix s[0..k−1] is a palindrome exactly when it equals its reverse, i.e., when it equals a suffix of rev(s) of length k. So we want the longest prefix of s that is also a suffix of rev(s). That is literally an LPS question: build t = s + "#" + rev(s) and the last value of its LPS array is k. The # stops the match from crossing the boundary (so k ≤ n).
Trace for s = "aacecaaa": rev = "aaacecaa", t = "aacecaaa#aaacecaa", last LPS value = 7, so the core is "aacecaa", the leftover is "a", answer is "a" + "aacecaaa".
notes: Say it like this: "The answer is the reverse of whatever follows the longest palindromic prefix, prepended to s. Checking every prefix is O(n²). A palindromic prefix of s equals a suffix of reverse(s), so the last LPS value of s + '#' + reverse(s) gives that length in O(n) time and space."
Edge cases: empty string (returns ""); already a palindrome (k = n, nothing added); all distinct characters like "abcd" → "dcbabcd".
Common mistakes: omitting the separator (for "aaa", "aaaaaa" has LPS 5 > n, which is wrong); appending to the end instead of the front; mixing up which part of rev to take.

Follow-ups: "Another linear approach?" Rolling hash: scan s once keeping a forward hash and a reverse hash of the prefix; the last index where they match is the longest palindromic prefix (verify to avoid collisions). Manacher's algorithm also gives it in O(n). "Add characters at the end instead?" Run the same idea on the reversed string (longest palindromic suffix).
simple: Add the fewest characters to the front to make the string a palindrome.

approaches.label: Brute Force
steps: For k from n down to 1, check whether s[0..k−1] is a palindrome (two pointers).
The first (largest) palindromic k wins; return reverse(s[k..]) + s.
approaches.why: Up to n prefixes, each checked in O(n); the output string is O(n).
approaches.simple: Find the longest prefix that is a palindrome by checking from the longest down.

approaches.label: Optimal
steps: rev = reverse(s), t = s + "#" + rev.
Build the LPS array of t; k = lps[t.length − 1].
Return rev.substring(0, n − k) + s (the first n − k chars of rev are exactly the reversed leftover).
approaches.why: LPS of a string of length 2n + 1 is linear, and so are t and the LPS array.
approaches.simple: Build s + # + reverse(s) and use KMP's LPS array to get the longest palindromic prefix in one pass.
